narrative: Today's digest centres on behavioural and landscape-scale responses to environmental change. In Journal of Animal Ecology, wolves were shown explicitly balancing risk and foraging benefit around active wildfires and smoke, one of the first fine-scale looks at large-carnivore behaviour during fire events, while reptiles in post-fire landscapes face narrower thermal activity windows as shelter buffering breaks down. A Landscape Ecology study of Eurasian pygmy owls found boreal populations held home ranges roughly twice the size of their Alpine counterparts, with photoperiod and landscape structure driving the difference despite both populations remaining strict forest specialists. Urban ecology findings were prominent: avian functional diversity in green spaces responded strongly to blue-green connectivity rather than green cover alone, and great tits across six European cities showed paler carotenoid plumage with increasing impervious surface. Century-long herbarium and photographic records revealed strongly season-dependent flowering responses to warming in tropical plants, with spring- and summer-flowering species delaying and autumn-winter species advancing. A horizon-scanning exercise for the Canary Islands prioritised dozens of candidate invasive species by environmental and socioeconomic risk, while isolated forest fragments in agricultural catchments were shown to meaningfully buffer stream biodiversity and function from upstream and downstream deforestation.
